summary: The article provides largely accurate information regarding ITR-4 deductions and presumptive taxation for TY 2026-27, with most claims verified against official and financial sources.

claims.claim: ITR-4 is for resident individuals, HUFs, and firms (other than LLPs) whose total income does not exceed ₹50 lakhs and who have opted for the Presumptive Taxation Scheme under Sections 44AD, 44ADA, or 44AE.
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm the eligibility criteria for ITR-4, including the income limit and the entities covered.

claims.claim: Section 44AD: Applicable to resident individuals, HUFs, and partnership firms (excluding LLPs) engaged in eligible businesses, with a total turnover or gross receipts not exceeding ₹3 crore in the previous year. Under this section, income is presumed to be 8% of the total turnover or gross receipts. However, if the receipts are received digitally (e.g., via bank transfer, UPI), the presumptive rate is reduced to 6% for that portion of the turnover.
claims.note: The turnover limit of ₹3 crore for Section 44AD, with the 6% for digital receipts and 8% for others, is consistently stated across sources, provided cash receipts are within 5% of total gross receipts.

claims.claim: Section 44ADA: Designed for resident individuals and partnership firms (excluding LLPs) engaged in specified professions, with gross receipts not exceeding ₹75 lakhs in the previous year. For these professionals, 50% of the total gross receipts are deemed as their net taxable income.
claims.note: The gross receipts limit of ₹75 lakhs for Section 44ADA, with 50% deemed as net taxable income, is accurate, especially with the condition of cash receipts not exceeding 5% of total receipts.

claims.claim: Section 44AE: Covers individuals, HUFs, and firms (other than LLPs) who own not more than 10 goods carriages at any time during the previous year and are engaged in the business of plying, hiring, or leasing such goods carriages. A fixed amount per vehicle per month is deemed as income under this section.
claims.note: Sources confirm the eligibility criteria for Section 44AE, including the limit of not more than 10 goods carriages and the fixed presumptive income per vehicle.

claims.claim: Section 80C, 80CCC, 80CCD (1): This is one of the most popular sections, allowing a combined deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakhs.
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm the combined deduction limit of ₹1.5 lakhs under Sections 80C, 80CCC, and 80CCD(1).

claims.claim: Section 80CCD (1B): An additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 for contributions to NPS Tier-I, over and above the ₹1.5 lakh limit of Section 80C.
claims.note: Sources confirm the additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 for NPS Tier-I contributions under Section 80CCD(1B), separate from the 80C limit.

claims.claim: Section 80TTA/80TTB: Section 80TTA allows a deduction of up to ₹10,000 on interest earned from savings bank accounts for individuals and HUFs. Section 80TTB, applicable to senior citizens, allows a deduction of up to ₹50,000 on interest income from savings accounts, fixed deposits, and recurring deposits.
claims.note: Sources confirm the deduction limits for Section 80TTA (₹10,000 for individuals/HUFs on savings interest) and Section 80TTB (₹50,000 for senior citizens on various interest incomes).

claims.claim: If you opt for the presumptive taxation scheme in a financial year, and then opt out of it in any of the subsequent five financial years, you will not be eligible to opt for the presumptive taxation scheme for the next five financial years. In such a scenario, you would also be required to maintain books of accounts and get them audited as per Section 44AB. This rule, primarily under Section 44AD, is significant and requires careful planning.
claims.note: The 'five-year rule' for opting out of presumptive taxation under Section 44AD, and the consequence of maintaining books and audit under Section 44AB, is accurately stated.
